tldr: By directly embedding tactile semantics—specifically which finger or palm is making contact—into visual point clouds, this research achieves an end-to-end pipeline from initial dexterous grasp pose generation to real-time adaptive refinement after contact. It achieved an 83% grasp success rate on unseen object categories and demonstrated stable grasping on a real-world robot.
hero_caption: Overall concept of the proposed method. On the left, an initial grasp is planned by predicting per-finger contact locations (contact map) from the object point cloud. Even when the initial grasp is loose and about to fail (top right), the system dynamically refines finger placement into a stable grasp in real time (bottom right) using a unified point cloud representation that fuses actual tactile feedback with geometric information.
overview:
Object grasping with multi-fingered dexterous hands is a longstanding challenge in robotics. Humans visually plan a rough hand shape, and upon touching the object, unconsciously adjust their grip force and finger positions based on tactile sensations to prevent slippage. In contrast, conventional robotic grasping predominantly relies on open-loop planning from camera images or point clouds, making it unable to handle misalignments and slips after contact occurs. While an increasing number of studies leverage tactile sensing, most simply concatenate feature vectors, failing to fully exploit the spatial and geometric correspondences of which finger touches where on the object.

To tackle this, the authors devised a "3D visuo-tactile representation" that directly maps contact information for each finger and the palm along with tactile intensity onto visual point clouds. Centered on this representation, they constructed "AdaDexGrasp," a unified framework integrating three components: an initial pose generator based on contact map prediction, a classifier predicting whether the current grasp is stable, and an adaptive model that refines the pose guided by tactile feedback.

Evaluation was conducted both in the massively parallel simulator IsaacGym and on a real-world robot arm and dexterous hand. The method achieved an 83% success rate in simulation on unseen object categories not encountered during training, and demonstrated high stability across 26 diverse real-world objects. It neatly demonstrates that treating tactile signals as a geometric spatial representation rather than a mere numerical vector leads to strong generalization performance.
contributions: Proposed a novel 3D visuo-tactile representation that associates finger and palm IDs and tactile intensity with individual points in a point cloud, enabling fine-grained reasoning about finger-object contact interactions.
Constructed a closed-loop grasping framework that integrates contact-aware initial grasp generation, post-contact feasibility prediction (classifier), and tactile-guided pose adaptive refinement.
Built a tactile-equipped dexterous hand training and evaluation simulation environment in IsaacGym, establishing an efficient dataset collection pipeline from PPO reinforcement learning rollouts.

Demonstrated in simulation and real-robot experiments that the method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines across a wide range of objects, including unseen objects and unseen categories.

sections.heading: Why is vision alone not enough for dexterous hands?
sections.summary: Humans grasp diverse objects dexterously by planning with vision and finely adjusting in real time with touch. This paper proposes a unified representation focusing on spatial visuo-tactile correspondence, solving initial planning through post-contact adaptation within a single framework.
sections.details:
When a human picks up a cup or a toy, they visually estimate the shape, decide roughly where to place their fingers, and reflexively adjust upon contact—such as pressing the thumb inward if it feels like it might slip. In contrast, existing robotic research has predominantly relied on vision-only, open-loop planning using RGB images or 3D point clouds. When surfaces are slippery or shapes are complex, slight misalignments at the moment of contact cause the grasp pose to collapse and fail.

While methods using tactile sensing do exist, many simply concatenate feature vectors in a deep learning latent space, missing the 3D geometric correspondences of which finger touches which location and with how much force.

This work introduces a unified representation that directly associates finger and palm semantics (part IDs) and tactile intensities with point cloud data. With this, the initial planning stage predicts a contact map specifying where each finger should touch to generate a reliable pose. After contact, the system evaluates grasp feasibility from point clouds incorporating actual sensor readings and executes real-time pose refinement in an adaptive closed loop when needed.

sections.heading: Current landscape of dexterous grasping and visuo-tactile fusion
sections.summary: Dexterous grasping research broadly splits into reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and object-centric visual methods, but all lack post-contact feedback. Furthermore, existing visuo-tactile fusion remains limited to simple feature concatenation or raw signals, suffering from spatial and geometric inconsistencies.
sections.details:
Research in dexterous hand grasping falls mainly into three approaches:
- Reinforcement Learning (RL): Acquires control policies through trial and error, but the search space is vast and training often becomes unstable.
- Imitation Learning (IL): Transfers human demonstration data to robots, but struggles to adapt flexibly to contact states not present in the demonstrations.
- Object-Centric Approaches: Plan grasps based on RGB-D camera observations and proprioception (joint angles); however, even if a grasp looks visually correct, it easily fails once contact becomes unstable on slippery surfaces.

Recently, studies combining vision and touch have emerged. Yet most either encode each modality into latent vectors via separate encoders and sum them up, or simply concatenate raw data. This fails to preserve spatial consistency and cannot accurately capture micro-scale interactions between fingertips and object surfaces. This work addresses this issue fundamentally by spatially embedding tactile signals directly into the object's 3D point cloud, bridging the gap between vision and touch.

sections.heading: The algorithm: from contact map prediction to closed-loop refinement
sections.summary: The proposed framework consists of three elements: a contact-driven initial pose generator, a classifier predicting feasibility from tactile-fused point clouds, and an adaptive model that refines unstable grasps. Efficient paired data collection from PPO exploration trajectories enables closed-loop guidance toward stable grasps.
sections.details:
The pipeline of this method consists of the following three main components linked together in a closed loop:

3.1 Problem Formulation
The target object $\mathcal{O}$ is represented as a point cloud $\mathcal{P}_{obj}$ obtained from an RGB-D camera. The robot hand state is $s=[p,q,\mathbf{j}]$, which includes the wrist translation, rotation, and 22 joint angles. Using 6 tactile sensor readings $\tau$ located on the 5 fingertips and the palm, the goal is to find the optimal state $s^*$ that maximizes the grasp success probability.

3.2 Overall Framework
A contact map and an initial pose are predicted from the input point cloud. After executing contact, tactile information is acquired. Based on this information, the classifier assesses stability; if it fails to meet the threshold, the adaptive model outputs a delta $\Delta s$ to update the pose.

3.3 Contact-Aware Grasp Pose Generator
Because tactile data does not exist before contact, PointNet++ is first used to predict a contact map $\mathcal{M}$ indicating which finger (or the palm) each point on the object surface should touch. Next, taking the object point cloud and this $\mathcal{M}$ as input, it regresses an initial pose $s_0$. Mediating through the semantics of finger part assignments allows the system to generate physically sound hand configurations from the start.

3.4 Grasp Pose Classifier
After executing the initial pose and establishing contact, a "visuo-tactile point cloud $\mathcal{P}_{vt}$" is created by assigning contact part IDs and tactile intensities to the object point cloud based on sensor values (contact forces). The classifier takes this $\mathcal{P}_{vt}$ and the hand point cloud as input and predicts the grasp success probability $\hat{y} \in [0, 1]$ in real time using Cross-Entropy loss.

3.5 Grasp Pose Adaptation Model
When the classifier predicts a likely failure, it predicts an adjustment $\Delta s$ to update the pose. During training, supervision pairs were formed from RL exploration trajectories by pairing "a state $s^f$ that failed right before" with "its geometrically and kinematically closest successful state $s^s$." By performing nearest-neighbor retrieval combining wrist SE(3) distance and joint-angle geodesic distance, the model efficiently learns natural, minimal corrective motions.

3.6 Closed-Loop Optimization and Data Collection
With a maximum iteration count of $K=5$ and a success threshold of $\tau_{succ}=0.5$, refinement repeats until judged successful. For data collection, PPO was run in IsaacGym, assigning tactile labels to point cloud regions where contact force exceeded 0.01N, automatically generating diverse grasp success and failure patterns.

A contact map is predicted from the object point cloud to execute an initial grasp, and tactile signals obtained after contact are mapped back onto the point cloud. If the classifier predicts failure, the adaptation model finely adjusts the pose to guide it toward a stable grasp.

The generator (green) outputs the contact map and initial pose, the classifier (yellow) evaluates stability via dual encoders and multi-head attention, and the adaptation model (blue) generates refined poses through denoising with a diffusion model.

sections.heading: Striking generalization demonstrated in simulation and real-world experiments
sections.summary: Comparative evaluations against 10 baselines were conducted in IsaacGym simulation and on a real dexterous hand setup. The proposed method achieved an 83% success rate on unseen categories not seen during training, vastly outperforming existing methods.
sections.details:
4.1 Experimental Setup
IsaacGym was used for simulation, modeling a ShadowHand with a total of 28 degrees of freedom (6-DoF wrist + 22 joints). 50 objects selected from UniDexGrasp++ were used (20 for training, 30 for testing). A grasp is considered successful if the object is lifted and held for 1 second without slipping.

4.2 Baseline Comparison
The method was compared against 10 baselines, including recent generative, RL, and VLA methods such as DexDiffuser and UniDexGrasp++. Vision-only generative methods frequently broke down on complex shapes, and conventional tactile methods using simple global feature concatenation failed to prevent micro-slipping.
The proposed method achieved extremely high success rates: 91% on trained objects (Seen), 82% on novel objects from trained categories (Unseen Objects), and 83% on completely novel categories (Unseen Categories). While baselines dropped to the 30–50% range on unseen categories, our method exhibited overwhelming robustness. It also maintained an 87% success rate on the large-scale "DexGraspAnything" dataset containing over 15,000 object instances.

4.3 Ablation Study
Evaluating the presence of contact IDs and the adaptation mechanism revealed that removing the adaptation model dropped the success rate on unseen categories from 83% to 59%—a 24-point plunge. Collapsing contact IDs into a single binary contact flag degraded both generation and adaptation accuracy, proving that knowing which finger is in contact is indispensable.

4.4 Real-World Experiments
Evaluations on 26 diverse real-world objects were conducted using a 7-DoF arm and an 11-DoF hand equipped with tactile sensors (Psibot SynHand-6). Even under a strict criterion of holding the lift for 3 seconds, the system demonstrated excellent adaptive behavior similar to simulation, confirming strong Sim-to-Real transferability.

4.5 & 4.6 Tactile Representation Choice and In-Depth Analysis
Overly rich tactile representations including shear forces drastically increased data requirements and widened the Sim-to-Real gap; a simple 6-dimensional per-finger contact intensity vector proved optimal (real-world success rate: proposed representation 85% vs. dense representation 72%). Furthermore, clear correlations emerged between object size, number of contacting fingers, and mean tactile intensity, with data confirming that successful grasps feature more fingers making contact evenly.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: This research enables high-precision, adaptive dexterous hand grasping through a representation that tightly binds geometric information and tactile signals. Unifying contact-aware initial planning with a real-time adaptation loop presents a scalable path toward future dexterous robot manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper introduced a novel representation directly fusing finger and palm tactile feedback onto 3D object point clouds, alongside the closed-loop grasping framework "AdaDexGrasp."

Predicting contact maps dramatically improves the viability of initial poses, while unexpected shifts and slips occurring after contact are swiftly corrected by a tactile-guided adaptation model. Thorough evaluations across simulation and real robots demonstrated exceptional generalization capability even on unseen object categories.

Integrating vision and touch as spatial contact semantics represents an important milestone, with promising applications beyond grasping to more advanced, complex dexterous manipulation tasks such as tool use and assembly.

sections.heading: Inference speed, hardware independence, and adaptation convergence
sections.summary: The supplementary material reports critical real-world operational details: real-time performance (20–25 Hz), versatility across left and right arms, and adaptation step counts. Over 90% of trials requiring refinement converged within 3 loop iterations.
sections.details:
The paper's Supplementary Material provides several key insights directly relevant to real-world deployment:

- Real-Time Capability and Inference Speed: Optimizing the Diffusion Policy backbone yields an overall system inference frequency of 20–25 Hz. This allows the system to adjust poses in real time even if an object shifts or begins to slip during lifting.
- Memory Footprint: While the full IsaacGym simulation consumes roughly 16 GB of GPU memory, standalone inference on the real robot requires only about 2 GB, easily running on standard edge GPUs.
- Adaptation Convergence: Pose refinement was triggered in approximately 30% of all trials. Among those cases, over 90% converged to a successful state in fewer than 3 iterations, demonstrating fast and efficient optimization.
- Hardware Independence: While main experiments were conducted using a left arm, the supplement presents results with the hand mounted on a right arm. Because processing is performed in an object-centric coordinate frame, the system achieves comparable grasp stability without retraining, regardless of mounting position or arm kinematics.

captions.F8: Qualitative visualization of initial grasp pose generation in simulation. Even for asymmetric, hard-to-grasp shapes like dolls, brushes, and tape measures, the model generates poses where fingertips and palm roles are appropriately assigned.

takeaways: Directly embedding touch into visual point clouds as spatial contact labels (part ID + intensity)—rather than treating it as a global feature vector—is exceptionally effective.

Decoupling the task into initial planning via contact map prediction and adaptive refinement via tactile feedback stabilizes training for dexterous hands with vast search spaces and yields high generalization to unseen objects.

Rather than pursuing high-dimensional tactile signals (such as shear forces and slip directions), adopting a simpler contact intensity representation with smaller simulation-to-real discrepancy is a practical design choice that improves Sim-to-Real transfer success.
limitations: For large objects approaching the physical size limit of the hand, grasping tends to fail because the fingers cannot wrap around the object.
For objects with extremely small contact areas or rapid dynamic friction changes during lifting, static contact intensity alone may not allow adjustments fast enough to prevent dropping.

Tactile sensor placement is restricted to the fingertips and palm (6 locations in total), so complex contact states like power grasps utilizing finger phalanxes (intermediate joints) are not sufficiently modeled.
